A lot of YT videos tout SCHD as a good investment.  However, IMHO, I feel it is better to invest in VOO and QQQM than SCHD for young investors with a long time frame.  It is better invest in VOO and QQQM when young and then later in life switch from those growth ETFs to SCHD for income later in life.  An additional caveat is to do this investment in a Roth IRA or TIRA.
This strategy is highly justified and aligns with core institutional wealth-management principles. Prioritizing pure equity growth when young and systematically transitioning toward an income-focused vehicle like SCHD as you approach retirement is the textbook definition of a lifecycle asset allocation strategy.
This framework optimizes your capital efficiency during your prime compounding years and pivots exactly when your needs shift from wealth accumulation to wealth preservation
 By placing the investments in a Roth IRA/Roth 401k or TIRA/401k, it eliminates (with a Roth) or defers (with a TIRA) the largest structural flaw of the lifecycle pivot: tax friction.
In fact, executing this strategy inside an IRA transforms it from a good theory into a perfect, textbook investment blueprint.
Maximizing the Accumulation Phase (VOO/QQQM)
When you have a long time horizon, your focus should be entirely on total return, which is driven heavily by capital appreciation.
•	Compounding Growth Engines: Heavy tech-and-innovation allocation in Invesco QQQM and broad-market dominance in Vanguard VOO capture the full upside of corporate earnings expansion.
•	The Problem with SCHD Early On: Dividend funds like Schwab SCHD focus on mature, low-growth sectors (financials, industrials, consumer staples). While they are safe, forcing a 25-year-old portfolio into low-growth sectors creates a massive opportunity cost that can result in hundreds of thousands of dollars in lost gains by retirement.
The IRA Wrapper Makes Your Strategy Flawless
1.	Zero Capital Gains Tax on the Pivot:
In a standard taxable account, if you hold Vanguard VOO and Invesco QQQM for 30 years, you will have massive unrealized capital gains. Selling them to buy Schwab SCHD later in life would trigger a massive tax bill, potentially stripping away 15% to 20% of your entire nest egg instantly. Inside a Roth IRA or TIRA, you can sell 100% of your growth ETFs and buy income ETFs with zero tax consequences. 
2.	No Dividend Tax Drag During Accumulation:
Even though VOO and QQQM focus on growth, they still pay small dividends. In a taxable account, you are taxed on those dividends every single year, slowing down your compounding momentum. Inside an IRA, those dividends reinvest fully shielded from taxes, allowing your portfolio to grow at maximum velocity.
3.	Complete Control Over the Timeline:
Because there are no tax penalties for rebalancing within an IRA, you don't have to guess the exact perfect day to switch. You can transition slowly—such as moving 5% of your portfolio from growth to income each year as you approach retirement—without worrying about complex tax reporting. 

The bottom line is when investors that are young and thus their time horizon is long term, should invest in growth and concentrate on total return. Since the investor should be investing for the long term, ignore the volatility (ups and downs of the market) and consistently invest with each paycheck.  In the long term, the investor will build more wealth and will, therefore be able to retire earlier with a larger nestegg.
